The experimental paradigm consisted of an emotional faces task ( Hariri et al., 2000 ; Lieberman et al., 2007 ) ( Figure 1 ).

description.value: Participants viewed target faces or shapes and performed emotion labeling, gender labeling, emotion matching, gender matching, and shape matching.

spans.text: Participants viewed target faces or shapes while performing one of five tasks
Emotion labeling involved choosing which of two labels (e.g., “angry,” “happy,” “scared,” “surprised”) described a target face.

description.value: Participants viewed a target emotional face and chose which of two labels (angry, happy, scared, or surprised) best described the face; this was treated as an incidental form of emotion regulation.

spans.text: Emotion labeling involved choosing which of two labels (e.g., “angry,” “happy,” “scared,” “surprised”) described a target face.

description.value: Participants viewed a target emotional face and chose which of two faces displayed the same emotion.

spans.text: Emotion matching involved choosing which of two faces displayed the same emotion as a target face.

description.value: Participants viewed a target face and selected the gender-appropriate name.

spans.text: Gender labeling involved selecting the gender-appropriate name for a target face.

description.value: Participants viewed a target face and selected which of two faces was the same gender.

spans.text: Gender matching involved selecting which of two faces was the same gender as a target face.

description.value: Participants viewed a target shape and selected which of two shapes was the same as the target shape.

spans.text: Shape matching involved selecting which of two shapes was the same as a target shape.

instructions.value: Participants viewed target faces or shapes and selected the matching label, gender, face, or shape: emotion labeling required choosing which of two emotion labels described a target face; gender labeling required selecting the gender-appropriate name; emotion matching required choosing which of two faces displayed the same emotion; gender matching required selecting which face was the same gender; and shape matching required selecting which of two shapes matched the target shape.
